page: Amazon Web Services c3.2xlarge is a compute-optimized, third-generation server instance. It features an x86_64 architecture powered by an Intel Xeon E5-2680 v2 processor running at 2.8 GHz. The configuration includes 8 vCPUs mapped to 4 physical cores with hyper-threading enabled, providing dedicated CPU allocation. The processor is equipped with 25 MB of L3 cache and supports AVX and AES instruction sets, though it lacks newer extensions such as AVX-512, AMX, and SHA-NI.

The instance is provisioned with 15.0 GB of system memory, yielding 1.88 GB of RAM per core. Local storage consists of a bundled 160 GB NVMe SSD, and network connectivity is established with a baseline bandwidth of 1 Gbps. No complimentary public IPv4 addresses are included in this configuration.

Performance benchmarks indicate average multi-core capabilities, with stress-ng multi-core CPU performance, Passmark CPU, and Passmark database operations all scoring in the middle 50% tier. Memory bandwidth tests for both cached and uncached operations also fall into the average range. However, single-core performance is weak, with Geekbench single-core scores in the bottom 10% and stress-ng single-core performance in the bottom 25%. Cryptographic and compression tasks show mixed results, with Passmark CPU encryption scoring average, while gzip compression and bzip3 decompression are weak.

Given its hardware profile and benchmark results, the c3.2xlarge is suited for legacy multi-threaded workloads, software compilation, and static web serving, where its average multi-core performance can be leveraged. It is less optimal for single-threaded applications, modern cryptographic workloads requiring advanced instruction sets, or large-scale LLM inference.
description: Amazon Web Services c3.2xlarge is a third-generation, compute-optimized instance featuring an Intel Xeon E5-2680 v2 processor with 8 vCPUs, 4 physical cores, and a 2.8 GHz clock speed. It is equipped with 15.0 GB of RAM, a bundled 160 GB NVMe SSD, and a 1 Gbps baseline network interface. Operating on the Xen hypervisor, this x86_64 server supports AVX and AES instructions but lacks AVX-512 and AMX capabilities. Benchmark data shows average performance in multi-core CPU execution, memory bandwidth, and static web serving, contrasted by weak single-core performance and poor results in modern LLM text generation. The instance represents a legacy hardware profile with dedicated CPU allocation, making it suitable for moderate multi-threaded workloads, software compilation, and basic database operations rather than high-performance single-threaded or modern AI tasks.
